hero.headline: Russian national linked to Delray Beach Medicare fraud company charged in second billing scheme
hero.teaser: A Russian national named Nika Machutadze, previously linked to Sunshine Senior Solutions in Delray Beach, allegedly continued billing Medicare through a Texas company after the original company lost its payments.
hero.body:
A Russian national connected to a Delray Beach durable medical equipment company accused of Medicare fraud allegedly continued billing the federal health program through a new business after the original company lost its payments. Nika Machutadze was charged with conspiracy to commit money laundering in January 2026 and arrested in Texas the following month. He remains in jail while federal prosecutors in West Palm Beach move forward with the case. Business records for both Sunshine Senior Solutions and Centurion Superior Medical list Machutadze as an owner.

Mike and Connie Parrett were among dozens of Medicare recipients who reported fraudulent billing after Sunshine Senior Solutions charged Medicare for medical equipment Connie said she never needed or received. "I hadn't even been to a doctor for anything," Connie said about the charges. More than a year later, the Parretts received a new Medicare statement at their Ohio home, this time in Mike's name, from Centurion Superior Medical, a company based in Austin, Texas. "But it's the same kind of thing. It's billing catheters, and actually there were six different bills," Mike said. Federal investigators have connected Centurion to the same operators behind Sunshine Senior Solutions.

A criminal complaint alleges Centurion billed Medicare in 2025 after federal authorities suspended payments to Sunshine Senior Solutions in late 2024. Two of the six charges from Centurion on Mike Parrett's statement were denied, though all charges occurred during 2025. Experts warn that victims of one fraud scheme often become targets for additional schemes. "As we've seen in this case, the criminals work with lists of identities and oftentimes they will just share the identities with other fraudsters," said Dr. David Maimon, a cyberfraud expert who studied Sunshine Senior Solutions.

Maimon recommends that potential victims freeze their credit and consider purchasing identity protection plans. He also pointed to the Justice Department's new National Fraud Enforcement Division, which investigates Medicare fraud cases. "This is all suggesting my opinion that we definitely take the issue of fraud more seriously," Maimon said. The repeated targeting of the same individuals demonstrates the ongoing challenge Medicare fraud poses to vulnerable seniors and the importance of government oversight in protecting beneficiaries.

cards.headline: 24-year-old technician killed after vehicle falls off lift at Stuart tire shop
cards.teaser: A 24-year-old technician died Tuesday morning after a customer's vehicle fell off a lift at Atlantic Tire at 705 Southeast Monterey Road in Stuart.
cards.body: A 24-year-old technician was killed Tuesday morning after a customer's vehicle fell off a lift at Atlantic Tire at 705 Southeast Monterey Road in Stuart. Stuart police responded to the incident, and Martin County Fire Rescue's extrication team arrived just after 6:30 a.m., finding the technician pinned between the vehicle and the wall inside the mechanic bay. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Stuart police say OSHA is involved and the incident is being investigated as a workplace incident.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor charged with child neglect after foster children found without food, functioning bathroom
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce pastor faces five counts of child neglect after authorities discovered five foster children living in severe conditions without proper food access or bathroom facilities. Gwendolyn Rolle, 59, had been caring for the children, ages 4 to 9, after their father placed them in her custody. On June 2, police responded to her home following reports of abuse.

When officers arrived, Rolle's daughter opened the door and confirmed that abuse was occurring in the home. According to the arrest affidavit, the daughter had hesitated to speak out earlier because of Rolle's standing in the community. Investigators found that the foster children were denied access to the home's working bathroom, which was kept locked. Instead, the children were forced to use a bucket for their bathroom needs and bathed outdoors using a garden hose on the front porch.

Police documented physical abuse during their investigation. One child had visible bruising on their chest, and multiple children reported being struck in the face or head during discipline. While officers were still at the home, one child said Rolle threatened them after arriving, telling the child that once police left, they would "get it." Beyond physical abuse, the children described inadequate meals. They reported frequently missing dinner or going to bed hungry. Major Michael Santiago of the Fort Pierce Police Department noted that the foster children depended on meals provided by neighbors to supplement their diet. Additionally, two of the children are non-verbal and attended a special needs school, but Rolle could not identify which school they attended or provide basic information about their education.

Following the investigation, the Department of Children and Families took custody of all five foster children. Rolle was released on bond pending trial. Major Santiago characterized the case as exhibiting unmistakable signs of neglect, describing the situation as "absolutely disgusting and tragic" for the children involved.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County faces nearly $400 million in budget cuts over two years under property tax proposal
cards.teaser: County Administrator Joe Abruzzo announced that if the property tax reduction passes, the budget for 30 departments could drop from $609 million to approximately $210 million, a loss of more than 65% of current funding.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County officials are bracing for what could be the largest budget cuts in the county's history, as proposed property tax reductions threaten to eliminate nearly $400 million from county operations over the next two years. County Administrator Joe Abruzzo announced during a budget meeting that if the property tax reduction passes, the county's budget for 30 departments could drop from $609 million to approximately $210 million, a loss of more than 65% of current funding. The Palm Beach County Fire Department alone stands to lose just under $200 million in funding under the proposed tax structure. Despite the magnitude of the proposed reductions, Abruzzo expressed confidence in the county's ability to continue operations, saying the cuts would not throw any types of services out of whack and would be extremely fiscally responsible.

A major concern centers on the proposed $250,000 homestead exemption, which may not represent the final figure. Abruzzo warned commissioners the exemption could potentially increase to $500,000, further deepening the budget shortfall. County leaders are examining millage rates and identifying cost-saving opportunities, with particular attention on the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office budget, which has increased more than 216% over the past 20 years. To help offset the shortfall, commissioners agreed to implement beach parking fees as a revenue-generating measure. Commissioners will set the maximum millage rate in July at 4.5, with final property value estimates and the complete budget scheduled for approval in September.

cards.headline: Vero Beach woman, 71, killed in four-car crash on I-95 near Mims
cards.teaser: A 71-year-old Vero Beach woman was killed in a four-car crash on Interstate 95 near Mims on Tuesday.
cards.body:
A 71-year-old Vero Beach woman was killed in a four-car crash on Interstate 95 near Mims on Tuesday. The collision occurred on the northbound lanes of I-95 in Brevard County.

Authorities responded to the scene of the multi-vehicle accident that involved four cars. The Vero Beach woman was pronounced dead at the scene.

The Florida Highway Patrol is investigating the circumstances that led to the crash. The incident caused delays on the northbound lanes of I-95 near the Mims area.

No further information about the other drivers involved or the cause of the collision has been released by authorities.

cards.headline: Boca Raton faces $16.7 million annual revenue loss under Florida property tax reform
cards.teaser: Deputy City Manager James Zervis outlined how the property tax referendum would reduce city revenues by $8.14 million in the first year and $16.7 million in the second year, forcing officials to explore alternative revenue sources.
cards.body:
City leaders in Boca Raton were briefed on Tuesday on the potential impact of property tax reform in Florida. Mayor Andy Thompson said the city will face an annual reduction of almost $17 million in two years, which he described as significant. Deputy City Manager James Zervis presented during a council workshop, outlining how two random homes in the city would likely see a reduction of property taxes of around $2,000 a year. However, revenues for the city would drop $8.14 million in the first year and $16.7 million in the second year.

The referendum before voters this November would raise the homestead exemption in 2027 to $150,000 and $250,000 in 2028. Zervis told the council that assuming the referendum passes, the city will definitely need policy direction on how to bring different ideas together and deal with the lost revenue issue. Policy direction involves exploring other sources of revenue, such as higher fees and other taxes, cuts in services and even raising the millage rate on property taxes. Thompson said the projected shortfall in a budget of around $250 million is significant but manageable. He said the city will take a hodgepodge approach rather than using one mechanism, testing out a bunch of mechanisms to address the shortfall.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast Square Mall redevelopment study draws mixed reactions from shoppers and business owners
hero.body:
Treasure Coast Square Mall has served the community for decades, but a redevelopment discussion initiated in 2023 has prompted questions about the facility's future direction. Martin County commissioned a study that year to examine potential changes to the mall, including the addition of apartments, an amphitheater, and green space designed in an outdoor format. County officials emphasized that the study was a planning exercise rather than a commitment to specific changes.

Community shoppers hold varied perspectives on the mall's current state and potential improvements. Liz Permar described the mall as "always been a fun place to go to," while Kimberly Grucza acknowledged it as acceptable but not her preferred destination. Despite their different views, both shoppers expressed support for updates to the facility. Permar said an update would be positive, and Grucza indicated that a facelift would benefit the mall. However, not all residents embrace every redevelopment concept under consideration. Grucza expressed concern about the proposed apartments, noting that the area already has numerous residential options.

Business owners operating inside the mall are closely monitoring the redevelopment discussions due to potential impacts on their operations. Jessica Henry, owner of Plantitude and Flame, expressed hope that any changes would maintain an open concept format for stores. Ron Gustafson, owner of MVP Sport Cards, reported that his store has performed well at its current location, stating the mall store model "has been tremendously successful." However, Gustafson also identified maintenance concerns, including water leaking into his store. He believes the mall requires attention and investment but could recover with proper effort and management, saying it is "in neglect" but "could turn around" with the right approach.

The path forward for Treasure Coast Square remains uncertain. Both Martin County Administrator Don Donaldson and Treasure Coast Square itself issued statements affirming that the 2023 study was only a planning exercise and does not necessarily indicate upcoming changes. Whether this study will eventually lead to actual redevelopment depends on decisions yet to be made. The mall's significance as a long-standing community institution means any substantial modifications would likely affect both the shoppers who frequent it and the business owners who depend on it for their livelihoods.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Town Council approves new rules limiting Mar-a-Lago helipad use to Trump presidential business
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach Town Council unanimously approved a fifth amendment outlining that the helipad shall be used exclusively for transporting President Trump for business related to the presidency only during his second term.
cards.body:
Council members in Palm Beach met Tuesday to approve new rules governing helipad use at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club. The helipad, approved in October, will measure 60 feet in diameter and sit on the west lawn, the same location as during Trump's first term. In April, the Secret Service requested the helipad remain in place even after Trump leaves office. The Palm Beach Town Council unanimously approved the revised fifth amendment by a 5-0 vote to address who can use the helipad and penalties for misuse.

The measure specifies that while Trump serves his second term, the helipad shall be used exclusively for transporting Trump for business related to the presidency only. After his second term ends, the helipad shall be used exclusively by government aircraft for emergency use of Trump or Melania Trump, as determined by the U.S. Secret Service with Secret Service personnel onboard. In emergencies, federal, state or local law enforcement, fire-rescue, emergency medical service, or other first responder agencies may use the helipad. All other use is strictly prohibited, including use by Mar-a-Lago members or guests, private parties, other protectees, or non-protectee Trump family members. Violations result in a $15,000 fine payable within 10 days, increasing by $10,000 for each subsequent violation. Construction begins this summer while the club is closed.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Turtle Tuesday beach cleanup enters 20th season to protect sea turtle nesting habitat
cards.teaser: The community-led beach cleanup known as Turtle Tuesday returns for its 20th season, having removed over 14,000 pounds of debris from Palm Beach beaches since 2006.
cards.body:
Tuesday marks the start of the 20th season for Palm Beach's community-led beach cleanup known as Turtle Tuesday. What began in 2006 as a small team-building activity has grown into a two-decade movement uniting local residents, businesses, and ocean lovers to protect sea turtles and restore critical nesting habitats. Founder Gregg Beletsky still remembers those humble beginnings. Since its inception, Turtle Tuesday volunteers have removed over 14,000 pounds of debris from Palm Beach beaches, including washed-up plastics and one notably odd find: a toilet seat. Collected trash is cataloged with the help of Loggerhead Marinelife Center, and the town of Palm Beach picks up the debris after the cleanups.

Turtle Tuesday is strategically scheduled during sea turtle nesting season and run in partnership with both the Town of Palm Beach and Loggerhead Marinelife Center to protect fragile habitats when it matters most. The group meets on the second Tuesday of every month from June through October, from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m., at the north end of Palm Beach Island at Mediterranean Road and North Ocean Way. Gloves, trash bags, and other cleanup supplies are provided. Participants are encouraged to bring sunscreen, a hat, and a reusable water bottle. Students can earn community service hours while participating. Beletsky said the mission is more pressing than ever, even after 20 years of work.

cards.headline: England's World Cup team trains in Palm Beach Gardens after win over New Zealand
cards.teaser: England's national soccer team is using facilities in Palm Beach Gardens for training after securing a 1-0 win over New Zealand in Tampa, with manager Thomas Tuchel praising the quality of the venue.
cards.body:
The England World Cup team is training in Palm Beach Gardens after defeating New Zealand 1-0 in a pre-World Cup friendly in Tampa over the weekend, with Harry Kane scoring the only goal. Manager Thomas Tuchel said the team expects to push on "physical and from intensity and style of play, ball speed and everything, want to take the next step." Tuchel praised the quality of the facilities in Palm Beach Gardens. Star defender Marc Guehi echoed those comments, saying "Everyone is super friendly and welcoming to us, felt at home straight away here, and in West Palm Beach. The quality of the pitch, really good so far."

Guehi addressed the challenge of adjusting to Florida's summer heat, noting "First day was extremely hot. We've been doing better getting used to the weather, getting used to the conditions, definitely a big step for us." At Gardens District Park, fields are watered before practice to help the ball skip across the grass rather than catching and rolling, allowing players to replicate stadium conditions. Palm Beach Gardens Director of Agronomy Andrew Keller explained the technique helps players "play faster so they can replicate what happens in the stadium." England plans to leave South Florida for Kansas City this weekend, with their first World Cup match against Croatia next Wednesday. Portugal's national team is also scheduled to train on the same fields.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County implements 45-day anchoring limits in Indian River Lagoon and Fort Pierce Harbor
cards.teaser: St.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County implemented new restrictions for boaters anchoring in county waterways on June 1. The county established two anchor limitation areas in the Indian River Lagoon and Fort Pierce Harbor near the South Causeway Bridge. Under the new rules, a person may not anchor a vessel for more than 45 consecutive days in any six-month period in any anchoring limitation area without leaving all anchoring limitation areas for at least 24 hours.

Erick Gill with St. Lucie County said the county has been seeing more abandoned vessels in these waterways. Last year, FWC collected around two dozen derelict vessels. Gill said the new restrictions will help make the waterways more navigable and ensure that the highway for vessels remains clear and free for other vessels to come and go. James Beams with St.Lucie County Port, Inlet and Beaches said abandoned vessels sitting for too long could impact water quality due to concerns with diesel and oil tanks and holding tanks. Gill said the restrictions will help avoid those pollutants from getting into the water. Over 4,000 species of animals, plants and birds live in the lagoon, Gill said, and the county wants to make sure it is protecting it.

cards.headline: Mom Mobile brings prenatal care to Okeechobee County where no hospital delivers babies
cards.teaser: A mobile clinic called Mom Mobile is bringing prenatal care directly to expecting mothers in Okeechobee County, which does not have a hospital that delivers babies.
cards.body:
Okeechobee County has no hospital that delivers babies, forcing many pregnant women to travel to Fort Pierce or Highlands County for care. The Mom Mobile program is bringing prenatal services directly to expecting mothers in the community. The 38-foot mobile clinic, which started with the Martin County Healthy Start Coalition, is stationed at the public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday.

Twenty-year-old Evelyn Allen discovered the program after struggling to find affordable resources in rural Okeechobee County. "I couldn't find any resources and the resources I did find you have to come out of pocket for it, or they would expect you to do more and you can't," Allen said. The need for Mom Mobile became immediately apparent. Fifteen women were seen during the first three days of operation, with appointment requests continuing to grow. Andrea Medellin with the Okeechobee Healthy Start Coalition said visits are designed as hour-long appointments intentionally focused on quality care for high-risk and underserved mothers. Allen calls the program a blessing.

cards.teaser: MorseLife announced a multi-county expansion of its PACE and behavioral health services and has integrated an AI health pilot into its PACE program.
cards.body: MorseLife announced a multi-county expansion of its PACE and behavioral health services. The organization has integrated an AI health pilot into its PACE program as part of the expansion. The expansion covers multiple counties in Florida, bringing additional health services to seniors in the region.

hero.headline: Wellington Wolverines football targeting playoff return after drought since 2022
hero.teaser: Wellington High School's football team is working through summer preparations with the goal of ending a postseason drought that has stretched since 2022.
hero.body:
Wellington High School's football program is working hard during summer training sessions to break a playoff drought that has lasted since 2022. The Wolverines are determined to return to postseason play this fall, and both players and coaches are committed to making it happen. The team's hunger for success is evident as they prepare for the upcoming season with focused training and team building.

The motivation among the players is strong. Senior Brady Seider expressed how meaningful a playoff appearance would be to the program. "It would mean everything you know. Everybody just looks at Wellington like we are a bunch of nobodies. We really wanna prove everybody wrong. We just wanna get there, see what it's like to win," Seider said. The team is tired of being overlooked and wants to show what they can accomplish on the field. This desire to prove doubters wrong is driving the Wolverines as they prepare for the season ahead.

Second-year head coach Pete Walker brings significant experience and success to the Wellington program. Walker previously captured three state titles while coaching at Glades Day, demonstrating his ability to build winning teams. He is confident in the current group's potential. "Well, first I had great coaches, which I have again on my staff. I think we're as good as anybody in Florida right now. The kids bought in through hard work and team and those types of things. So that's the things that we're concentrating on again, and they're moving in the right direction," Walker said. His leadership and the quality of his coaching staff are major assets for the program.

Junior Danhoi Williams emphasized that the summer work is about establishing a strong foundation for success. "Just trying to get a winning season and try to go to the playoffs. You know, get them gelling, new teammates, new coaches. Just trying to see that everything is going right in the summer and head into the season with it," Williams said. The team is focused on building chemistry, integrating new players and coaches, and ensuring everything is in place before the fall season begins. As summer workouts continue, the Wolverines are preparing themselves to compete and achieve their goal of returning to the playoffs.

cards.headline: 24-year-old technician killed after vehicle falls off lift at Stuart tire shop
cards.teaser: A 24-year-old technician died Tuesday morning after a customer's vehicle fell off a lift at Atlantic Tire at 705 Southeast Monterey Road in Stuart.
cards.body: A 24-year-old technician was killed Tuesday morning after a customer's vehicle fell off a lift at Atlantic Tire at 705 Southeast Monterey Road in Stuart. Stuart police responded to the incident, and Martin County Fire Rescue's extrication team arrived just after 6:30 a.m., finding the technician pinned between the vehicle and the wall inside the mechanic bay. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Stuart police say OSHA is involved and the incident is being investigated as a workplace incident.

cards.headline: England's World Cup team trains in Palm Beach Gardens after 1-0 win
cards.teaser: England's national team trained at Gardens District Park in Palm Beach Gardens Tuesday following a 1-0 victory over New Zealand in Tampa over the weekend.
cards.body:
The England national team is training in Palm Beach Gardens after securing a 1-0 victory over New Zealand in a pre-World Cup friendly in Tampa over the weekend. Harry Kane scored the winning goal with a header. Before the World Cup begins, England has another tuneup match scheduled in Orlando. Manager Thomas Tuchel discussed the team's preparation, saying "We expect to push tomorrow physical and from intensity and style of play, ball speed and everything, want to take the next step." Tuchel also praised the quality of the facilities in Palm Beach Gardens.

Star defender Marc Guehi echoed those comments about the accommodations and venue. "Great, fantastic. Everyone is super friendly and welcoming to us, felt at home straight away here, and in West Palm Beach. The quality of the pitch, really good so far," Guehi said. He also addressed adapting to Florida's summer heat, noting "First day was extremely hot. We've been doing better getting used to the weather, getting used to the conditions, definitely a big step for us." At Gardens District Park, Palm Beach Gardens Director of Agronomy Andrew Keller explained that fields are watered before practice to help the ball move faster across the grass. England plans to leave for its Kansas City base camp this weekend, with the team's first World Cup match against Croatia scheduled for next Wednesday. Portugal's national team will also train on the same fields after England's departure.

cards.headline: Mom Mobile brings prenatal care to Okeechobee County every Tuesday
cards.teaser: A 38-foot mobile clinic has started offering prenatal care at the Okeechobee public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday, helping expecting mothers in a county with no delivery hospital.
cards.body:
For expecting mothers in Okeechobee, getting prenatal care isn't always easy. The county has no hospital that delivers babies, forcing many women to travel to Fort Pierce or Highlands County for care. Mom Mobile, a program that started with the Martin County Healthy Start Coalition, is bringing prenatal services directly to expecting mothers and their families in Okeechobee. Twenty-year-old Evelyn Allen discovered the program after learning she was pregnant. "You know I was just getting my life on track and then boom, out of nowhere. I would say it was a very big surprise," she said. Living in rural Okeechobee County, Allen struggled to find affordable resources. "I couldn't find any resources and the resources I did find you have to come out of pocket for it, or they would expect you to do more and you can't."

The 38-foot mobile clinic is stationed at the public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday, designed to offer care in a safe and welcoming environment. During the first three days of operation, fifteen women were seen, with appointment requests continuing to grow. Andrea Medellin with the Okeechobee Healthy Start Coalition explained the clinic's approach: "This bus looks like an hour-long visit for moms. It's intentional, it's specifically set not to serve more but to serve quality for our high-risk and need moms." Allen calls the service a blessing, saying "I've gotten really lucky with this place."

cards.headline: DAS Beer Garden in Jupiter plans World Cup street party and free beer for USA goals
cards.teaser: DAS Beer Garden at 1203 Town Center Drive in Jupiter is promising free beer for every Team USA goal and a street party for the World Cup Final.
cards.body:
DAS Beer Garden in Jupiter is preparing for the FIFA World Cup with free beer for every Team USA goal and a street party for the final match. Co-owner Alex Marquez said the World Cup brings an energy unlike any other sporting event. "When the World Cup starts, it's just different. You can just see the vibe changes, everybody gets really into it," Marquez said. He noted that the tournament carries a deeper meaning for fans than a typical match. "Now it's your country. It's your blood, it's your heritage," Marquez said.

Marquez said the lower-scoring nature of soccer is part of what makes watching it so electric. "Sometimes it's less scoring. But a lot of people believe that's a bad thing. I think that's a good thing because the expectation of that score builds up so much that when that happens, that's when you see people not pretending to lose their minds, but really losing their minds," Marquez said. Soccer fan Jason Pitman plans to attend the bar's morning watch parties, saying he will be "one of those people at 9 a.m. eating those donuts that Alex brings in." For the World Cup Final, DAS Beer Garden plans to shut down Town Center Drive and set up a big screen television across the street for an outdoor soccer street party. The tavern is located at 1203 Town Center Dr 116 in Jupiter.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Turtle Tuesday beach cleanup marks 20th year of protecting sea turtle nesting
cards.teaser: The community-led beach cleanup known as Turtle Tuesday began its 20th season Tuesday, meeting monthly at the north end of Palm Beach Island to remove debris during nesting season.
cards.body:
Tuesday marks the start of the 20th season for Turtle Tuesday, a community-led beach cleanup protecting sea turtles and restoring critical nesting habitats in Palm Beach. What began in 2006 as a small team-building activity has grown into a two-decade movement uniting local residents, businesses, and ocean lovers. Founder Gregg Beletsky remembers those humble beginnings. Since its inception, Turtle Tuesday volunteers have removed over 14,000 pounds of debris from Palm Beach beaches, including washed-up plastics and one toilet seat, the strangest item found during cleanups. Collected trash is cataloged with help from Loggerhead Marinelife Center, and the town of Palm Beach picks up the debris after cleanups.

Turtle Tuesday is strategically scheduled during sea turtle nesting season and run in partnership with the Town of Palm Beach and Loggerhead Marinelife Center to protect fragile habitats when it matters most. The group meets on the second Tuesday of every month from June through October, from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m., at the north end of Palm Beach Island at Mediterranean Road and North Ocean Way. Gloves, trash bags, and other cleanup supplies are provided. Participants are encouraged to bring sunscreen, a hat, and a reusable water bottle. Students can earn community service hours while participating.

cards.headline: 6.1 magnitude earthquake off Cuba felt in Florida, evacuations in Miami
cards.teaser: A 6.1 magnitude earthquake off the west-northwest coast of Cuba prompted evacuations of several buildings across Miami on Tuesday and was felt as far north as Jacksonville.
cards.body:
A 6.1 magnitude earthquake off the west-northwest coast of Cuba prompted evacuations of several buildings across Miami on Tuesday and was felt as far north as Jacksonville. Students at Fusion Academy were among those evacuated, with some reporting they felt the tremors more intensely on higher floors. "We usually hear the fire alarm, like the beam, beam, beep, but this one was very like evacuate now, like they were saying this is not a drill, so it was really scary," student Maria Torrado said.

Not everyone detected the earthquake. Students at the Swatch Watchmaking School were evacuated but initially had no idea why. "We literally didn't feel a thing. We thought maybe somebody was messing with them," Jack Hodapp said. Streets near some affected buildings were blocked off while the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office set up a command center. Those evacuated were let back inside shortly after. Juan Cardona initially thought the commotion was a criminal scene before learning from others that an earthquake in Cuba had impacted the Florida area. The National Weather Service said there is no tsunami risk as a result of the quake, and no injuries have been reported.

hero.headline: Cornell Art Museum in Delray Beach opens upcycled art exhibit running through September
hero.teaser: The Cornell Art Museum at Old School Square has opened Persistence of Matter, a summer exhibition spotlighting artists who turn discarded materials into sculptures and mixed media pieces.
hero.body:
The Cornell Art Museum at Old School Square in Delray Beach is showcasing "Persistence of Matter," a new summer exhibition dedicated to artists who transform discarded materials into compelling artwork. The show reflects the museum's commitment to blending artistic expression with positive community engagement, according to Marusca Gatto, Cultural Arts Director for the Delray Beach Downtown Development Authority. Guest curators Mavis Benson and Pamela Lambie selected artists creating sculptures, installations, and mixed media works entirely from reclaimed objects.

The exhibition highlights several notable artists, including Autumn Kioti, whose creations draw inspiration from both natural and urban environments. Another featured artist, Mike Silverman, presents his "Self-Reflection" series, which transforms discarded computer hard drive platters and printed circuit boards into reflective sculptures. Silverman explained that his pieces are designed to help viewers reconsider their relationship with technology and waste, inviting them to see themselves reflected in materials typically destined for landfills.

As environmental concerns grow across communities, this exhibition serves as a visual conversation about sustainability and responsible consumption. "Persistence of Matter" demonstrates how artistic innovation can highlight the ongoing life cycles of discarded materials while promoting environmental awareness through creative beauty. The show encourages visitors to think differently about waste and its potential for transformation into meaningful art.

The exhibition runs through September 10, 2026, and includes several programming opportunities for deeper engagement. Visitors can attend artist talks, participate in salon discussions, and watch film screenings throughout the exhibition period. The museum maintains regular hours: Wednesday noon to 5 p.m., Thursday and Friday noon to 7 p.m., Saturday 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday noon to 5 p.m. For more information about upcoming events and programs, visitors can call 561-654-2220.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach to host finish of 80-mile ocean paddle race for cystic fibrosis June 13
cards.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June to raise awareness and funds for families living with cystic fibrosis in the ann.
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June to raise awareness and funds for families living with cystic fibrosis in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. According to event founder Travis Suit, participants will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The endurance trek benefits the Piper's Angels Foundation, which Suit established in honor of his daughter, Piper, diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing begins June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night. All paddlers are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, and crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during a daylong beach celebration marking their arrival. More information is available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

hero.headline: Agriculture budget passes with Florida delegation split on food assistance programs
hero.teaser: Several Florida congressional members touted passage of an agriculture budget that includes citrus health funding, but every Florida Democrat voted against the legislation citing cuts to food assistance programs.
hero.body:
The Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act passed the House on a narrow 213-210 vote, with Florida's congressional delegation divided along party lines. Republican supporters highlighted the bill's benefits for the state's agricultural sector. Rep. Scott Franklin, a Lakeland Republican, said the legislation strengthens agricultural research and animal and plant health programs while addressing threats like bird flu and invasive pests. He emphasized that agriculture remains central to Central Florida's economy and way of life, noting that farmers face challenges from rising costs, foreign competition, and severe weather.

The bill allocates $72 million for citrus health response, with $11 million specifically targeting citrus greening disease. Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart, a Hialeah Republican and Vice Chair of the House Appropriations Committee, praised the legislation for ensuring the safety of food and medical products while reinforcing consumer protections. He also highlighted provisions that strengthen national security by safeguarding against foreign agricultural interests and prioritizing research to keep the domestic agricultural sector competitive. Rep. Vern Buchanan, a Longboat Key Republican, secured $2 million to combat animal fighting, calling it a brutal practice linked to criminal activity.

However, every Florida Democrat voted against the legislation, citing concerns about food assistance programs. Rep. Frederica Wilson, a Miami-Dade Democrat, said the bill fails to fully fund the Women, Infants, and Children program and threatens access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. She warned that these cuts harm pregnant women and babies while weakening support for vulnerable Americans. Wilson also objected to provisions she described as targeting LGBTQ individuals and families. Rep. Greg Steube, a Sarasota Republican, also voted against the budget, objecting to funding for organizations including Save the Children and CARE, which he said promote initiatives he opposes, including LGBTQ advocacy and abortion access.

Rep. Daniel Webster, a Clermont Republican who supported the bill, secured $1.5 million for the City of Webster's Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program and championed language supporting the Rural Electrification and Telecommunications Loan Program. He characterized the legislation as supporting farmers and ranchers while promoting food safety and reducing reliance on foreign competitors like China.

cards.headline: Former House Speaker Paul Renner qualifies for gubernatorial ballot in Republican Primary
cards.teaser: Former House Speaker Paul Renner officially qualified Tuesday to be on the ballot for the August 18 Republican Primary for Governor, joining 11 other candidates in the race.
cards.body:
Former House Speaker Paul Renner officially qualified for the Aug. 18 Republican Primary for Governor by paying the $8,484 qualifying fee for party affiliated candidates. A Navy veteran and attorney, Renner first ran for the State House in Jacksonville in 2014, losing his primary by just two votes. He moved to a district further south the following year and won a Special Election, eventually serving nine years in the House, including a term as Speaker from 2022 to 2024. Renner has identified eliminating property taxes, blocking construction of AI Data Centers, border security and fighting corruption as his key issues.

According to recent polls, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds leads the Republican Primary field after securing President Donald Trump's "complete and total endorsement" in February 2025. Despite polling in the single digits, Renner has pointed to straw polls showing stronger support among the party's most engaged members. Renner has argued Donalds is weak and could lose to presumptive Democratic nominee David Jolly, a moderate who previously represented Pinellas County in Congress as a Republican before leaving the GOP in 2018 and registering as a Democrat in 2025. Jolly became the presumptive Democratic nominee after Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings dropped out to focus on his prostate cancer treatment. Candidates have until noon Friday to qualify, with the qualifying period having opened Monday.

cards.headline: Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert raises $250,000 in first five days of congressional campaign
cards.teaser: Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert reported raising more than $250,000 in the first five days after confirming his bid for Florida's 25th Congressional District.
cards.body:
Gilbert, a lawyer and former Miami Gardens Mayor who won re-election to the County Commission unopposed in 2024, announced last week that he will resign his District 1 seat effective January 3, 2027. His congressional campaign is centered on a "Put People First" agenda focused on expanding health care access, investing in public transit, making childcare universal and cutting taxes for working families. Federal campaign finance reports for the second quarter of 2026 are due July 15.

The 25th Congressional District as redrawn under a mid-decade redistricting plan drafted by Governor Ron DeSantis' office, passed by the Legislature in late April and signed in early May, covers Miami Gardens in Miami-Dade and Hollywood, Miramar and Pembroke Park in Broward County. More than 68.7% of voters there backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, making the Democratic Primary the race that will effectively determine who replaces retiring Democratic U.S. Representative Frederica Wilson. State Senator Shevrin Jones of Miami Gardens, former Miami-Dade Commissioner Jean Monestime, business owner Christine Sanon-Jules and physician Rudy Moise have filed for the contest ahead of the June 12 qualifying deadline. Miami-Dade School Board member Steve Gallon won election unopposed Tuesday to succeed Gilbert on the Miami-Dade Commission.

cards.headline: Governor DeSantis signs bills sending Hillsborough County government reforms to November ballot
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis signed two bills Monday that will let Hillsborough County voters decide in November whether to expand the County Commission and elect thei.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis signed two bills Monday that will send major Hillsborough County government reforms to the November 2026 ballot. The measures, sponsored by Apollo Beach Republican Rep. Michael Owen, ask voters whether to reshape county government and how the local school district chooses its superintendent. HB 4029 proposes expanding the Hillsborough County Commission from seven members to nine and eliminating countywide seats in favor of single-member districts. The board would later grow to 11 members if the county's population reaches at least 2.5 million residents. The proposal would also require a "majority plus one" vote of the full Commission for certain key actions, including appointing or removing the County Administrator, County Attorney and County Internal Auditor, and proposing charter amendments. It would revise the composition and appointment process for the county's Charter Review Board and alter rules for citizen-led charter amendments.

HB 4027 asks voters whether to replace the district's appointed superintendent with an elected one. If approved, the Hillsborough County Public Schools Superintendent would be chosen in a partisan countywide election beginning in 2028 and serve a four-year term. Supporters of both measures argue the current structure dilutes local representation in a county with more than 1.5 million residents and makes countywide races more expensive. The Superintendent proposal drew sharp debate, with supporters saying voters should have direct say over the leader of one of the state's largest school districts, while opponents warned it could politicize the role and pull focus from the district's educational mission.

cards.headline: Jacksonville City Council approves November referendum on school property tax extension
cards.teaser: Jacksonville voters will decide in November whether to extend a one mill property tax to boost teacher pay, after the City Council unanimously approved putting the measure on the ballot.
cards.body:
The Duval County School Board's effort to place a tax extension referendum on the November ballot succeeded Tuesday when the Jacksonville City Council unanimously voted to discharge the measure from committee. Ordinance 2026-387 would allow voters to decide whether to extend for four years a one mill ad valorem tax designed to boost teacher pay, continuing a levy first approved in 2022. Republican Raul Arias supported the discharge motion after meeting with School Board members, union representatives and Superintendent Chris Bernier. "Let the community decide what they want to do," Arias said. Democrat Tyrona Clark-Murray stated, "If you say no to this, you're saying no to children." Republican Mike Gay called the vote "the American way," while Republican Ron Salem said he was convinced after speaking with the Superintendent.

The property tax extension would continue if a majority of voters approves it in November. That threshold is lower than the 60 percent required for state ballot initiatives, including a homestead property tax amendment on the same ballot that would increase the exemption and take nearly $300 million out of city revenues. President-elect Nick Howland opposed the original 2022 push, saying other funding was available at that time, but noted that funds have since been depleted from the American Rescue Act.

cards.headline: Five Miami-Dade Commission members win unopposed as three districts head to August elections
cards.teaser: Four incumbent Miami-Dade Commission members and incoming member Steve Gallon coasted into office unopposed following Tuesday's qualifying deadline, while three other seats face August challengers.
cards.body:
Four incumbent Miami-Dade Commission members and one incoming member won their seats unopposed following the county's qualifying deadline Tuesday. Chair Anthony Rodriguez and Commissioners J.C. Bermudez, Natalie Milian Orbis and Micky Steinberg were re-elected without challengers. Steve Gallon, leaving the Miami-Dade School Board after serving since 2016, will succeed Commissioner Oliver Gilbert in District 1, which covers northern Miami-Dade including Miami Gardens. Gilbert is departing early to run for Congress. Gallon will serve the two remaining years on Gilbert's current term and is then eligible to run for re-election twice for four years apiece before reaching term limits.

Mayor Daniella Levine Cava congratulated the automatic winners in a statement, noting their party affiliations span the political aisle. "I am proud to work alongside these dedicated public servants as we continue building a stronger Miami-Dade County," she said. Rodriguez, a Republican first elected in 2020 to represent District 10, previously served as Vice Chair and as a Florida House member from 2018 to 2022. Bermudez, a Republican who won in 2022, represents District 12 and served as founding Mayor of Doral. Milian Orbis, a Republican and former Vice Mayor of West Miami, took her District 6 seat by appointment in early May 2025. Steinberg, a Democrat and former Miami Beach City Commissioner, won unopposed for a second consecutive election in District 4.

cards.headline: Longtime Tallahassee lawmaker Allison Tant draws Democratic Primary challenger
cards.teaser: Florida House member Allison Tant will face a Democratic Primary after Michael Sneed Jr. filed for her seat Tuesday, just three days ahead of the candidate qualifying deadline.
cards.body:
Allison Tant, a long-time Florida lawmaker representing areas in and around Tallahassee, will face a Democratic Primary challenge after Michael Sneed Jr. filed for her Florida House District 9 seat Tuesday, just three days ahead of the candidate qualifying deadline. Tant has become one of the more prominent Democrats in the House of Representatives since her election in 2020. She was a vocal advocate during last month's Special Session when she pushed for pay raises for state workers. Lawmakers ultimately approved some pay increases for law enforcement personnel, but not for general state government employees. Tant argued that such raises would have helped the economy in her district because many state employees are based in and around the state capital.

Sneed, a resident of Greenville about a half hour east of Tallahassee, has not yet qualified for the race or reported any fundraising activity. Tant has already amassed $246,993 in monetary contributions and spent about $10,600, according to state elections records. Originally from Neptune Beach on the First Coast, Tant has deep connections within Democratic politics. She served as Chair of the Florida Democratic Party from 2012 to 2016 and cast Florida's nominating votes at the 2016 Democratic National Convention. She is also a former lobbyist with Holland Knight and Steel, Hector and Davis International. The Democratic Primary winner will face one of two Republican candidates, Tracy Latroy Robinson or Jibri Knight. The qualifying deadline is Friday.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast Square Mall redevelopment study sparks mixed reactions in Martin County
hero.body:
Treasure Coast Square Mall remains a longtime community landmark, yet renewed discussion about its future has prompted questions from shoppers and business owners about what changes might mean for them. Martin County initiated a study in 2023 that examined potential redevelopment approaches, including residential apartments, an amphitheater, and outdoor green spaces. County officials have characterized the study as an exploratory planning exercise rather than a confirmed blueprint.

Community members express divided opinions about proposed updates. Shopper Liz Permar supports a renovation, calling it a positive step. Fellow shopper Kimberly Grucza also welcomes improvements but has reservations about certain proposals. While Grucza appreciates the concept of updating the mall, she opposes the idea of adding apartments to the property, citing the existing abundance of residential developments already in the area.

Business operators leasing space inside the mall are closely monitoring the redevelopment discussions. Jessica Henry, who owns Plantitude and Flame, hopes that any changes preserve the ability for businesses to continue operating within the property, preferably through expanded open-concept layouts. Ron Gustafson, owner of MVP Sport Cards, reports that his business has performed well at its current location. Despite this success, Gustafson has dealt with persistent water damage issues affecting his storefront. He believes the property requires significant maintenance and upgrades, stating that with proper effort and management, the mall could recover. "I think it's in neglect. I think with some effort and the right management I think this could turn around," Gustafson said.

Martin County Administrator Don Donaldson confirmed that the 2023 study remains what it was originally intended to be: a planning exercise. Officials have not indicated whether the county intends to pursue any of the redevelopment options explored in the study. For now, the future of Treasure Coast Square Mall remains uncertain, with community stakeholders awaiting clarity on whether the county will move forward with any concrete development plans.

cards.headline: 24-year-old technician killed after vehicle falls off lift at Stuart tire shop
cards.teaser: A tire shop employee was killed after a vehicle fell off a lift Tuesday morning at Atlantic Tire in Stuart. The incident is being investigated as a workplace accident.
cards.body: Stuart police responded to Atlantic Tire at 705 Southeast Monterey Road in Stuart after a customer's vehicle fell off a lift and fatally injured a 24-year-old technician Tuesday morning. Martin County Fire Rescue's extrication team arrived just after 6:30 a.m. and found the technician pinned between the vehicle and the wall inside the mechanic bay. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Stuart police say OSHA is involved and it is being investigated as a workplace incident.

cards.body: Irwin 'Cy' Louis Seidel of Palm City has died, according to Forest Hills Memorial Park & Palm City Chapel. Services are being handled by the funeral home.

cards.teaser: Mrs. Universe 2026 visited a Stuart nonprofit that supports people with disabilities.
cards.body: Mrs. Universe 2026 visited a Stuart nonprofit to support people with disabilities, according to reports. The visit highlighted the organization's work in the community.

cards.headline: Boca Raton studies impact of Florida property tax reform on city budget
cards.teaser: Boca Raton officials were briefed on the potential impact of property tax reform in Florida. The city could lose nearly $17 million annually within two years.
cards.body:
City leaders in Boca Raton were briefed on Tuesday on the potential impact of property tax reform in Florida. Mayor Andy Thompson said the city faces a $16 million to almost $17 million annual reduction in two years. Deputy City Manager James Zervis presented during a council workshop, outlining how two random homes in the city would likely see a reduction of property taxes of around $2,000 a year. However, revenues for the city would drop $8.14 million in the first year and $16.7 million in the second year.

The referendum before voters this November would raise the homestead exemption in 2027 to $150,000 and $250,000 in 2028. Zervis said the city will need policy direction on how to deal with the lost revenue issue, which involves exploring other sources of revenue such as higher fees and other taxes, cuts in services and raising the millage rate on property taxes. Thompson said the projected shortfall in a budget of around $250 million is significant but manageable. He said the city will take a hodgepodge approach and not rely on one mechanism, but will test out multiple options.

cards.headline: England's World Cup team trains in Palm Beach Gardens after win over New Zealand
cards.teaser: England's national soccer team is training in Palm Beach Gardens after securing a 1-0 win over New Zealand in Tampa. The team is preparing for the World Cup.
cards.body:
England's national team secured a 1-0 win over New Zealand in a pre-World Cup friendly in Tampa over the weekend, with Harry Kane's header providing the only goal. The team has another tuneup scheduled in Orlando before the tournament begins. Manager Thomas Tuchel said the team expects to "push tomorrow physical and from intensity and style of play, ball speed and everything, want to take the next step." Tuchel praised the quality of the facilities in Palm Beach Gardens, where the team is training. Star defender Marc Guehi echoed those comments, saying "Everyone is super friendly and welcoming to us, felt at home straight away here, and in West Palm Beach. The quality of the pitch, really good so far."

Guehi acknowledged the challenge of Florida's summer heat, noting "First day was extremely hot. We've been doing better getting used to the weather, getting used to the conditions, definitely a big step for us." At Gardens District Park, fields were watered before practice. Palm Beach Gardens Director of Agronomy Andrew Keller explained the practice helps "the ball skip across the field rather than the ball catching on the grass and rolling." England plans to leave for Kansas City this weekend. The team's first World Cup match is next Wednesday against Croatia. Portugal's national team is scheduled to train on the same fields after England's departure.

cards.headline: Vincent Stuart dies in St. Petersburg
cards.teaser: Vincent Stuart of St. Petersburg has died.
cards.body: Vincent Stuart of St. Petersburg has died, according to Tampa Bay Times obituary records. Services are being handled by the family.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce pastor charged with child neglect after foster children found without food, functioning bathroom
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce pastor faces five counts of child neglect after authorities discovered five foster children living in severe conditions without proper food access or bathroom facilities. Gwendolyn Rolle, 59, had been caring for the children, ages 4 to 9, after their father placed them in her custody. On June 2, police responded to her home following reports of abuse.

When officers arrived, Rolle's daughter opened the door and confirmed that abuse was occurring in the home. According to the arrest affidavit, the daughter had hesitated to speak out earlier because of Rolle's standing in the community. Investigators found that the foster children were denied access to the home's working bathroom, which was kept locked. Instead, the children were forced to use a bucket for their bathroom needs and bathed outdoors using a garden hose on the front porch.

Police documented physical abuse during their investigation. One child had visible bruising on their chest, and multiple children reported being struck in the face or head during discipline. While officers were still at the home, one child said Rolle threatened them after arriving, telling the child that once police left, they would "get it." Beyond physical abuse, the children described inadequate meals. They reported frequently missing dinner or going to bed hungry. Major Michael Santiago of the Fort Pierce Police Department noted that the foster children depended on meals provided by neighbors to supplement their diet. Additionally, two of the children are non-verbal and attended a special needs school, but Rolle could not identify which school they attended or provide basic information about their education.

Following the investigation, the Department of Children and Families took custody of all five foster children. Rolle was released on bond pending trial. Major Santiago characterized the case as exhibiting unmistakable signs of neglect, describing the situation as "absolutely disgusting and tragic" for the children involved.
